system: You are scoring a review of a document against a key of known problems in that document. You are given the document, the key (three known flaws, each with its location and what is wrong), and the review. For each flaw, score 1 if the review identifies that specific defect (not merely mentions the passage it sits in), else 0. Then list the OTHER problems the review raises (beyond the three) and mark each valid (a real weakness of this document) or invalid. Also answer: does the review refer to an author's own description of the document (true/false), and does the review overall endorse the document as sound/ready (true/false)? Reply with JSON only: {"flaws": {"1": 0|1, "2": 0|1, "3": 0|1}, "other": [{"issue": "...", "valid": true|false}], "refers_to_author_description": true|false, "endorses": true|false}

DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
**What the study claims.** A pilot with 4,000 households shows strong participation, similar across houses and flats, so a single uniform service can roll out district-wide. Projected tonnage is about 3,290 a year, all treated at Brookfield, 14 miles away. The net cost is about £490,000, which the provisional £520,000 new-burdens allocation covers in full.

**Verdict.** The service is a legal requirement, so the question is how to deliver it, not whether. On that, the study's operational core is sound. But three of its headline conclusions are contradicted by its own figures: participation was **not** similar across housing types, treatment is **not** all local, and the service is **not** clearly fully funded.

## What holds

- The pilot is well designed: a sensible caddy set-up, same-day collection, a mixed sample, and weekly measurement.
- Table 1 is internally consistent: 2,112 / 3,200 = 66%, 168 / 800 = 21%, 2,280 / 4,000 = 57%.
- Table 2 adds up. Vehicles: £990,000 / 7 = £141,400. Crews: 12 × £34,000 = £408,000. Total: £733,400. The £74 per tonne saving (£112 − £38) is correct.
- Contamination under 2% is a good result.

## What's wrong

**1. Participation was very different in flats.** It was **66% in houses against 21% in flats**, roughly a third of the rate. Flats that did take part also produced less (1.4 kg against 1.9 kg a week). The study says participation was "broadly similar," and builds its uniform-service recommendation on that.

The data point the other way: flats need their own approach, such as communal bins, different collection points and targeted communications. With about 10,400 flats in the district, this is a significant part of the roll-out.

**2. The projection uses a participation rate the pilot didn't produce.** §3 applies **64%**, which appears nowhere in the pilot data. The pilot's overall rate was **57%**. Projecting by housing type for the district:
- Houses: 41,600 × 66% × 1.9 kg
- Flats: 10,400 × 21% × 1.4 kg

That gives about **2,870 tonnes a year**, not 3,290. The pilot's 20% share of flats matches the district's, so the pilot-wide 57% gives the same answer.

**3. Brookfield can't take the projected tonnage.** Its contracted capacity is **1,800 tonnes a year until 2029**. Even the corrected 2,870 tonnes leaves about **1,070 tonnes** that must go to the plant 46 miles away, at an unstated gate fee and with longer journeys. Otherwise that waste isn't diverted from incineration at all. Yet the saving assumes every tonne goes to Brookfield at £38.

**4. The service is not shown to be fully funded.** Correcting the figures step by step:

| Scenario | Disposal saving | Net cost | Against £520k allocation |
|---|---|---|---|
| As written (3,290 t, all to Brookfield) | £243,000 | £490,000 | covered |
| Corrected tonnage (2,870 t, all to Brookfield) | ~£212,000 | ~£521,000 | short by ~£1,000 |
| Only 1,800 t diverted | ~£133,000 | ~£600,000 | short by ~£80,000 |

The likely outcome falls between the last two rows, depending on the second plant's gate fee and haulage costs. So the funding gap is somewhere between a few thousand pounds and about £80,000 a year, rather than a £30,000 surplus.

## Weakly supported or missing

- **Funding certainty.** The allocation is *provisional*, and its duration isn't stated. The £990,000 for vehicles and the cost of caddies fall due up front. The study should say whether new-burdens money covers capital costs and cash flow, or only annual running costs.
- **Possibly missing cost lines.** The author describes the costing as covering everything, but these don't appear:
  - cover for crew holidays and sickness, and a spare vehicle;
  - supervision and management;
  - staff for the dedicated phone line;
  - financing costs on the vehicles;
  - haulage to the second plant.
  Some of these may be included under "fuel and maintenance" or in the £34,000 per operative. If so, say so.
- **Fleet size.** Six vehicles serving 52,000 households weekly is about 1,700 households per vehicle per day. The pilot rounds should show whether that is realistic.
- **Timetable risk.** Ordering vehicles in December for March delivery assumes a short lead time at a moment when every English council is buying the same vehicles. Confirm with the supplier in writing. Delivering caddies to 52,000 households and recruiting and training 12 operatives in a single month is also tight.
- **Statutory date.** I understand the national requirement for household food waste collections took effect from 31 March 2026, with later dates agreed for some councils. Confirm that Thornbury's April 2027 start has been agreed.
- **The pilot evidence itself.**
  - It ran from January to June only, so seasonal yields and a drop in participation once the service is no longer new are both untested.
  - The survey response rate isn't given. The 81% satisfaction figure most likely comes from households that took part.

## Suggested changes before Cabinet

1. Revise §3 to project by housing type: about 2,870 tonnes.
2. Withdraw "uniform service" and add a separate approach for flats, with its own cost.
3. Add a treatment plan for the tonnage above 1,800, with a gate fee and haulage cost for the second plant. Alternatively, negotiate more Brookfield capacity before 2029.
4. Restate the net cost as a range, set against the provisional allocation, and flag the funding gap.
5. Confirm the vehicle lead time and the statutory start date.

The recommendation to proceed and order the vehicles can stand. The claims that the service is uniform, local and fully funded cannot.
